How it fits together

Every project pushes to the same registry. What keeps projects apart is not a separate registry each, and not a firewall — it is the repository namespace. Your pipeline gets an identity that can write to yourteam/ and nowhere else, and that boundary is enforced by Azure, not by convention.

The registry is reachable from the public internet on purpose. Hosted CI runners have no stable egress address, so locking the registry to an IP range would mean every team running self-hosted runners. Authorization does the work instead: there is no anonymous access, no shared admin password, and every pipeline authenticates as itself.

Piece What it is Where it lives
Registry One Premium Azure Container Registry, deployed with the Azure Verified Module for ACR infra/terraform
Tenancy Repository namespaces, enforced by ABAC conditions on role assignments infra/terraform
Identity One managed identity per pipeline, federated to your repository and branch infra/terraform
Pipelines The same seven steps for Azure DevOps, GitHub Actions and GitLab CI pipelines/
Scan policy A single Trivy configuration all three platforms load pipelines/common/trivy.yaml

You need three values before you start. All three come out of Terraform, and none of them is a secret — there is no registry password anywhere in this design.

terraform output 
cd infra/terraform

terraform output login_server            # contosocentralregistry.azurecr.io
terraform output azure_tenant_id         # your Entra tenant
terraform output -json ci_identities     # client_id per pipeline identity

Set up your project

Azure DevOps Pipelines

1. Create the service connection

In your Azure DevOps project, go to Project settings → Service connections → New → Azure Resource Manager → Workload Identity federation (manual). Enter the subscription and the client_id of your tenant's managed identity.

Azure DevOps then shows an Issuer and a Subject identifier. This is a two-step dance, because the service connection has to exist before its subject does: create the identity with a placeholder subject, create the connection with the resulting client ID, then paste the real issuer and subject back into Terraform and re-apply.

2. Register the identity

infra/terraform/terraform.tfvars 
tenants = {
  reporting = {
    display_name = "Reporting"

    ci_identities = {
      build = {
        access  = "push"
        issuer  = "https://vstoken.dev.azure.com/<organization-id>"
        subject = "sc://<organization>/<project>/acr-push"
      }
    }
  }
}

The subject is checked on every token exchange. Another project's service connection cannot use this identity even if it knows the client ID.

3. Add the pipeline

Copy the reference build assets from pipelines/common into your repository root — Dockerfile, trivy.yaml and .trivyignore — then add this as azure-pipelines.yml and edit the three values under parameters.

azure-pipelines.yml 
###############################################################################
# Copy this file into your project repository as azure-pipelines.yml and edit
# the values under `parameters:` in the extends block.
#
# The build itself lives in the central template, so a change to the shared
# scanning policy reaches every project without touching this file.
###############################################################################
trigger:
  branches:
    include:
      - main
  tags:
    include:
      - v*

pr:
  branches:
    include:
      - main

resources:
  repositories:
    - repository: container-ci
      type: github
      name: olljanat-ai/container-ci
      ref: refs/heads/main
      endpoint: github-container-ci # GitHub service connection name

extends:
  template: pipelines/azure-devops/templates/container-build.yml@container-ci
  parameters:
    registry: contosocentralregistry.azurecr.io

    # Must start with your tenant's namespace. Pushing outside it is denied by
    # the ABAC condition on the pipeline identity, not just by convention.
    image: payments/api

    # ARM service connection using workload identity federation, backed by the
    # managed identity Terraform created for this tenant.
    azureServiceConnection: acr-push

    # Optional; these are the defaults.
    # dockerfile: Dockerfile
    # buildContext: .
    # trivyConfig: trivy.yaml
    # trivySeverity: HIGH,CRITICAL
    # defaultBranch: refs/heads/main

The build itself lives in the shared template, so a change to the scanning policy reaches your project without you editing anything.

GitHub Actions

1. Register the identity

Add your project to var.tenants in Terraform. The subject has to match the token GitHub actually mints for the job:

infra/terraform/terraform.tfvars 
tenants = {
  payments = {
    display_name = "Payments platform"

    ci_identities = {
      build = {
        access  = "push"
        issuer  = "https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com"
        subject = "repo:contoso/payments-api:ref:refs/heads/main"
      }
    }
  }
}

GitHub issues a different sub claim for branches, tags, pull requests and each environment. Add one ci_identities entry per subject you build from, or federate on repo:<owner>/<repo>:environment:<name>, which stays stable across refs.

2. Add three repository variables

Under Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → Variables. These are identifiers, not credentials — they belong in variables, not secrets.

VariableValue
AZURE_CLIENT_IDclient_id from terraform output -json ci_identities
AZURE_TENANT_IDterraform output azure_tenant_id
AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_IDterraform output azure_subscription_id

3. Add the workflow

Copy the reference build assets from pipelines/common into your repository root — Dockerfile, trivy.yaml and .trivyignore — then add this as .github/workflows/container.yml and edit registry and image.

.github/workflows/container.yml 
###############################################################################
# Copy this file into your project repository as
# .github/workflows/container.yml and edit the four values under `with:`.
#
# It delegates the whole build to the central reusable workflow, so a change to
# the shared scanning policy reaches every project without touching this file.
###############################################################################
name: Container image

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    tags: ["v*"]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

# Two pushes to the same branch should not race each other into the registry.
concurrency:
  group: container-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  image:
    uses: olljanat-ai/container-ci/.github/workflows/build-and-push.yml@main

    # The called workflow cannot grant itself more than this.
    permissions:
      contents: read
      id-token: write # mint the OIDC token the federated credential accepts
      security-events: write # upload Trivy SARIF to code scanning

    with:
      registry: contosocentralregistry.azurecr.io

      # Must start with your tenant's namespace. Pushing outside it is denied
      # by the ABAC condition on the pipeline identity, not just by convention.
      image: payments/api

      # From `terraform output -json ci_identities`. These are identifiers, not
      # credentials, so repository variables are the right home for them.
      azure-client-id: ${{ vars.AZURE_CLIENT_ID }}
      azure-tenant-id: ${{ vars.AZURE_TENANT_ID }}
      azure-subscription-id: ${{ vars.AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID }}

      # Optional; these are the defaults.
      # dockerfile: Dockerfile
      # context: .
      # trivy-config: trivy.yaml
      # trivy-severity: HIGH,CRITICAL

The build itself lives in the shared reusable workflow, so a change to the scanning policy reaches your repository without you editing anything.

GitLab CI/CD

1. Register the identity

Add your project to var.tenants in Terraform. The subject has to match the ID token GitLab mints for the job:

infra/terraform/terraform.tfvars 
tenants = {
  web = {
    display_name = "Web frontend"

    ci_identities = {
      build = {
        access  = "push"
        issuer  = "https://gitlab.com" # your instance URL if self-managed
        subject = "project_path:contoso/web:ref_type:branch:ref:main"
      }
    }
  }
}

Tag pipelines produce ref_type:tag:ref:<tag>, so add a second entry if you build from tags.

2. Add two CI/CD variables

Under Settings → CI/CD → Variables — on the group, if several projects share the registry. Neither is a credential, so neither needs masking or protection.

VariableValue
AZURE_CLIENT_IDclient_id from terraform output -json ci_identities
AZURE_TENANT_IDterraform output azure_tenant_id

They are read at job runtime rather than passed as component inputs, because include:inputs is resolved before CI/CD variables exist.

3. Add the pipeline

Copy the reference build assets from pipelines/common into your repository root — Dockerfile, trivy.yaml and .trivyignore — then add this as .gitlab-ci.yml and edit registry and image.

.gitlab-ci.yml 
###############################################################################
# Copy this file into your project repository as .gitlab-ci.yml and edit the
# two values under `inputs:`.
#
# Also define two CI/CD variables, on the group if several projects share the
# registry (Settings -> CI/CD -> Variables):
#   AZURE_CLIENT_ID   from `terraform output -json ci_identities`
#   AZURE_TENANT_ID   from `terraform output azure_tenant_id`
# Both are identifiers rather than credentials - nothing here needs masking.
#
# The build itself lives in the central template, so a change to the shared
# scanning policy reaches every project without touching this file.
###############################################################################

# Run one pipeline per change: a merge request pipeline while the MR is open,
# a branch pipeline otherwise. Without this, GitLab creates both.
workflow:
  rules:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH && $CI_OPEN_MERGE_REQUESTS
      when: never
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_TAG

stages:
  - build

include:
  - project: contoso/container-ci
    ref: main
    file: pipelines/gitlab/templates/container-build.yml
    inputs:
      registry: contosocentralregistry.azurecr.io

      # Must start with your tenant's namespace. Pushing outside it is denied
      # by the ABAC condition on the pipeline identity, not just by convention.
      image: payments/api

      # Optional; these are the defaults.
      # dockerfile: Dockerfile
      # build_context: "."
      # trivy_config: trivy.yaml
      # trivy_severity: HIGH,CRITICAL
      # default_branch: main

The build itself lives in the shared component, so a change to the scanning policy reaches your project without you editing anything.

The build contract

All three platforms run these seven steps, in this order. The order is the point: the image is built on the runner and held there until every scan has passed, so a vulnerable image never lands in a registry that every project can read.

  1. Install Aikido Safe Chain Runner Shims npm, pnpm, yarn, pip, uv and poetry so every package the job installs is checked against Aikido Intel before it is written to disk.
  2. Scan the source with Trivy Gate Dependency CVEs from lock files, committed secrets, and Dockerfile misconfiguration — before anything is built.
  3. Build the image Runner Safe Chain is installed inside the Dockerfile's build stage as well, because npm ci inside docker build runs in the build container where the runner's shims do not exist.
  4. Scan the built image with Trivy Gate OS packages and application libraries in the finished image. This is the gate that keeps the shared registry clean.
  5. Generate a CycloneDX SBOM Artifact Kept with the build, so you can answer "which of our images ship this package" without rebuilding anything.
  6. Authenticate to Azure over OIDC Federated The job's own token is exchanged for an Azure token. No registry password exists in any CI system, so none can leak from one.
  7. Push Default branch and tags Pull and merge request builds run every scan but never push.

Image naming

The first path segment must be your namespace. A push outside it returns denied no matter what the pipeline asks for.

image reference 
contosocentralregistry.azurecr.io/payments/api:9f2c1ab34d5e6f7089abcdef0123456789abcdef
contosocentralregistry.azurecr.io/payments/api:latest        # default branch only
contosocentralregistry.azurecr.io/payments/api:v1.4.2        # tag builds

Every build is tagged with the full commit SHA, so a deployment always names an exact build. latest moves; the SHA tag never does.

Namespaces and access

The registry is one flat set of repositories, split by prefix. Your team owns a prefix; everyone can read the shared and cached ones. 

contosocentralregistry.azurecr.io
├── shared/                    golden base images — everyone reads, platform team writes
├── cache/                     pull-through cache of docker.io and mcr.microsoft.com
│   └── docker-hub/library/node
├── payments/api               payments team
├── payments/worker
└── web/frontend               web team

Each grant is an Azure role assignment on the registry carrying an ABAC condition that pins it to those prefixes. This is what the pipeline identity for the payments team actually holds:

ABAC condition, rendered by Terraform 
(
 (
  !(ActionMatches{'Microsoft.ContainerRegistry/registries/repositories/content/read'})
  AND
  !(ActionMatches{'Microsoft.ContainerRegistry/registries/repositories/content/write'})
  AND
  !(ActionMatches{'Microsoft.ContainerRegistry/registries/repositories/metadata/read'})
  AND
  !(ActionMatches{'Microsoft.ContainerRegistry/registries/repositories/metadata/write'})
 )
 OR
 (
  @Request[Microsoft.ContainerRegistry/registries/repositories:name] StringStartsWithIgnoreCase 'payments/'
 )
)

Read it as: unless the caller is performing one of these repository data actions this assignment says nothing; if they are, the repository name must start with payments/.

The trailing slash is load-bearing. Without it, payments would also match payments-archive/secrets. Terraform rejects a namespace that does not end in /.
Access Role assigned Own namespace shared/ and cache/ Other teams
pull Container Registry Repository Reader read read denied
push Container Registry Repository Writer read + write read denied
contribute Container Registry Repository Contributor read + write + delete read denied

Listing repository names is a separate role, Container Registry Repository Catalog Lister, which does not accept ABAC conditions — granting it exposes every repository name in the registry. It is opt-in per team with catalog_lister = true, and off by default.

Base images come from the cache

Pull base images through the registry instead of from Docker Hub. That takes the anonymous rate limit off the critical path of every build, and means an image your fleet depends on is stored somewhere you control.

Dockerfile 
ARG REGISTRY=docker.io
ARG NODE_IMAGE=${REGISTRY}/cache/docker-hub/library/node:22-bookworm-slim

FROM ${NODE_IMAGE} AS build

The pipelines pass REGISTRY as a build argument, so the same Dockerfile still builds on a laptop with no registry access.

What fails a build

One Trivy configuration is shared by all three platforms, so what blocks a build is a one-file decision rather than three drifting copies.

pipelines/common/trivy.yaml 
###############################################################################
# Shared Trivy configuration.
#
# Every pipeline in this repository points Trivy at this file (TRIVY_CONFIG or
# `--config`), so all three platforms enforce the same policy and a policy
# change is a one-file change.
#
# Reference: https://trivy.dev/latest/docs/references/configuration/config-file/
###############################################################################

timeout: 15m

scan:
  scanners:
    - vuln
    - secret
    - misconfig

# Findings at or above these levels fail the build. Anything lower is still
# reported in the SARIF/JSON output but does not block, so the gate stays
# actionable.
severity:
  - HIGH
  - CRITICAL

# Fail the step when a finding at or above `severity` survives the filters
# below. The report-only passes in the pipelines (SBOM, SARIF upload) override
# this back to 0 on the command line.
exit-code: 1

# End-of-life base images are reported but do not set a distinct exit code
# here: the pipelines run Trivy twice - once to produce a full SARIF report and
# once as the blocking gate - and a non-zero exit from the report pass would
# stop the results being uploaded. Set this to 1 in a scheduled job, or add
# `--exit-on-eol 1` to the gate step, if you want EOL distros to block.
exit-on-eol: 0

# Dismissed findings live in .trivyignore, each with an expiry date. The path is
# resolved relative to the working directory, not to this file - which is why
# trivy.yaml and .trivyignore both belong in your repository root, and why the
# pipelines run Trivy from there.
ignorefile: .trivyignore

vulnerability:
  # Only fail on vulnerabilities that have a fix available. An unfixable CVE in
  # a base image cannot be actioned by the team that owns the application, and
  # blocking on it teaches people to bypass the gate. Catch those separately
  # with a scheduled `--ignore-unfixed=false` run against the whole registry.
  ignore-unfixed: true

pkg:
  types:
    - os
    - library

misconfiguration:
  include-non-failures: false

db:
  no-progress: true
  # Trivy's vulnerability database is pulled from a container registry. If your
  # runners cannot reach ghcr.io, mirror the DB into the central registry and
  # point these entries at <login-server>/cache/... instead.
  repository:
    - mirror.gcr.io/aquasec/trivy-db:2
    - ghcr.io/aquasecurity/trivy-db:2

Why Trivy runs twice per target

The first pass writes a full-severity report — SARIF for GitHub code scanning and Azure DevOps artifacts, GitLab's own format for the merge request security widget. The second pass is filtered to HIGH,CRITICAL and is the one that fails the build. Splitting them keeps the gate actionable without hiding the long tail, and the vulnerability database is cached between the two, so the second pass costs little.

Why unfixable findings do not block

ignore-unfixed: true is a deliberate call. A CVE with no upstream fix cannot be actioned by the team that owns the application, and blocking on it only teaches people to bypass the gate. Catch those in a scheduled sweep with --ignore-unfixed=false across the whole registry, where the platform team can act on them.

Dismissing a finding

Put it in .trivyignore with an expiry and a reason. An entry without one is a finding nobody owns.

.trivyignore 
CVE-2024-00000 exp:2026-12-31
  No fix upstream; the affected code path is not reachable from our entrypoint.
  Owner: platform-team. Re-checked 2026-09-08.

Blocking malicious packages

Aikido Safe Chain runs a local proxy and routes package downloads through it, checking each one against Aikido Intel. A package that is known malware — at any dependency depth — is blocked before it reaches disk. It also suppresses versions published in the last 48 hours, which is the window where a compromised release does most of its damage.

Install it in two places, not one. The runner install covers what the job installs. It does not cover npm ci inside docker build — that runs in the build container, where the runner's shims do not exist. The reference Dockerfile installs Safe Chain in its build stage for exactly this reason.

Both installs pin a release version and verify the installer's SHA-256. GitHub release assets are immutable, so a versioned URL plus a checksum means the script that runs is the script that was published.

pipelines/common/Dockerfile 
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1.11
###############################################################################
# Reference Dockerfile for the central registry pipelines (Node.js).
#
# The build stage installs Aikido Safe Chain before it installs any
# dependencies. Safe Chain proxies npm through Aikido Intel, so a package that
# is known malware - or that was published in the last 48 hours and has not
# been vetted yet - is blocked before it reaches the image. Installing it on
# the CI runner is not enough on its own: `npm ci` inside `docker build` runs
# in the build container, where the runner's shims do not exist.
#
# The runtime stage carries neither Safe Chain nor the build toolchain.
###############################################################################

# Base images come from the registry's pull-through cache so builds do not
# depend on Docker Hub's anonymous rate limit. REGISTRY is passed by the
# pipeline; the default keeps the file usable outside CI.
ARG REGISTRY=docker.io
ARG NODE_IMAGE=${REGISTRY}/cache/docker-hub/library/node:22-bookworm-slim

ARG SAFE_CHAIN_VERSION=1.5.18
ARG SAFE_CHAIN_SHA256=bdbc58829853e598c09874fcc193f7cdb2a9a848875be45260a8b59bc4ce5439

###############################################################################
# Stage 1 - dependencies and build, behind Safe Chain
###############################################################################
FROM ${NODE_IMAGE} AS build

ARG SAFE_CHAIN_VERSION
ARG SAFE_CHAIN_SHA256

RUN apt-get update \
 && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends ca-certificates curl \
 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# `--ci` installs executable shims rather than shell aliases, which is what
# makes the interception work in a non-interactive RUN instruction.
RUN curl -fsSL "https://github.com/AikidoSec/safe-chain/releases/download/${SAFE_CHAIN_VERSION}/install-safe-chain.sh" -o /tmp/install-safe-chain.sh \
 && echo "${SAFE_CHAIN_SHA256}  /tmp/install-safe-chain.sh" | sha256sum -c - \
 && sh /tmp/install-safe-chain.sh --ci --install-dir /usr/local/safe-chain \
 && rm /tmp/install-safe-chain.sh

# The shims must precede the real npm on PATH.
ENV PATH="/usr/local/safe-chain/shims:/usr/local/safe-chain/bin:${PATH}"

# Fails the build if the shims are not actually in front of npm.
RUN npm safe-chain-verify

WORKDIR /app

COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm npm ci

COPY . .
RUN npm run build --if-present \
 && npm prune --omit=dev

###############################################################################
# Stage 2 - runtime
###############################################################################
FROM ${NODE_IMAGE} AS runtime

ENV NODE_ENV=production

WORKDIR /app

COPY --from=build --chown=node:node /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY --from=build --chown=node:node /app/dist ./dist
COPY --from=build --chown=node:node /app/package.json ./package.json

USER node
EXPOSE 3000

# Trivy's misconfiguration scanner flags images that run as root or omit a
# healthcheck, so both are set here.
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --start-period=10s --retries=3 \
  CMD node -e "fetch('http://127.0.0.1:3000/healthz').then(r => process.exit(r.ok ? 0 : 1)).catch(() => process.exit(1))"

CMD ["node", "dist/index.js"]

npm safe-chain-verify is in the build on purpose: if the shims ever stop landing ahead of the real npm on PATH, the build fails loudly instead of quietly installing unchecked packages.

Running the registry

The registry is one Terraform configuration built on the Azure Verified Module for Container Registry. Premium is not optional here: ABAC repository permissions, geo-replication, scope maps, cache rules, IP rules and the untagged-manifest retention policy are all Premium-only, and the tenancy model depends on the first of those.

deploy 
cd infra/terraform
cp terraform.tfvars.example terraform.tfvars   # then edit

export ARM_SUBSCRIPTION_ID=<subscription-id>
az login

terraform init
terraform plan
terraform apply

Adding a team

One entry in var.tenants, then apply. The namespace, the role assignments, the ABAC conditions and the pipeline identity all follow from it.

infra/terraform/terraform.tfvars 
tenants = {
  # ...existing teams...

  analytics = {
    display_name = "Analytics"

    ci_identities = {
      build = {
        access  = "push"
        issuer  = "https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com"
        subject = "repo:contoso/analytics:ref:refs/heads/main"
      }
    }
  }
}

Deliberate choices

SettingValueWhy
admin_enabled false A shared username and password that bypasses every namespace boundary
anonymous_pull false Cannot be scoped per team — it would expose every repository
public_network_access true Hosted runners have no stable egress IP; authorization does the isolation
role_assignment_mode AbacRepositoryPermissions Required for per-repository scoping. Legacy AcrPull/AcrPush are not honoured in this mode
retention_policy_in_days 30 Untagged manifests pile up fast when every commit produces an image
Switching an existing registry to ABAC mode is not a no-op. Legacy AcrPull, AcrPush and AcrDelete assignments stop being honoured, and credentials clients cached before the switch are rejected with HTTP 401 until they refresh. Assign the ABAC roles without conditions first, switch, force clients to refresh, then narrow the conditions.

When it breaks

No matching federated identity record found

AADSTS700213. The service connection's subject does not match subject in terraform.tfvars. Read it again from the service connection page — it changes if the connection or the project is renamed.

AADSTS70021. The token's subject does not match the federated credential. The usual cause is building from a tag or a pull request when the credential was federated on ref:refs/heads/main. Add an entry for that subject, or federate on an environment instead.

AADSTS70021. The token's subject does not match the federated credential. Print what the job actually sends and compare:

.gitlab-ci.yml 
echo "$AZURE_ID_TOKEN" | cut -d. -f2 | base64 -d 2>/dev/null | jq '{iss, sub, aud}'

denied: requested access to the resource is denied

The image name is outside your namespace, or the role assignment has not propagated yet. Check the first path segment of the image against terraform output tenant_namespaces. ABAC changes usually take effect within a minute or two, but a token minted before the change keeps its old permissions until it expires.

ResourceNotFound from az acr login

Expected, and the reason the pipelines do not use az acr login. It resolves the registry through the ARM control plane first, which needs Microsoft.ContainerRegistry/registries/read — a permission the pipeline identities deliberately do not have. The pipelines exchange the Entra token for an ACR refresh token directly instead, which needs no control-plane access at all.

unauthorized when pulling a base image

Base images must come through <login-server>/cache/…, and your identity needs read access to cache/ — which it has by default. If you are pulling from docker.io directly, you are hitting Docker Hub's anonymous rate limit rather than an authorization problem.

A build fails on a CVE you cannot fix

Check whether it is actually unfixable: the gate already ignores findings with no available fix. If there is a fix and you cannot take it yet, add a .trivyignore entry with an expiry date and an owner, and open the work to remove it. Do not lower severity in your copy of trivy.yaml — that hides the next finding too.

Container CI — platform engineering Rendered from the pipeline files themselves by tools/build_docs.py
